I'm an epidemiologist at a public health institute in Ahmedabad, writing in a personal capacity. An editor at a national English daily has offered me 900 words on heat action plans before summer. My problem: I have too many findings, and my draft opens with 'India's heat action plans are failing,' which I'm not sure I can defend and which will annoy the municipal officials I need to keep working with.

These are from our analysis of 2019-2024 mortality data across four mid-sized cities in Gujarat and Rajasthan:

1. Excess deaths during heat waves were 38% lower in 2024 than in 2019, so the plans have helped overall
2. But 61% of excess deaths now occur on day 1 and day 2 of a heat wave
3. Current plans trigger the highest (red) alert only after 3 consecutive days above threshold
4. Night-time minimum temperature was a better predictor of excess deaths than daytime maximum (r = 0.71 vs 0.48)
5. Outdoor informal workers (construction, street vending, waste picking) were 3.2x over-represented in day 1-2 deaths
6. Cooling centres in two of the cities were open 10am-5pm only
7. Awareness of the heat plan among surveyed outdoor workers: 23%
8. Hospital preparedness improved: ORS stocks and cold rooms now in 80% of district hospitals

Current opening paragraph:
'India's heat action plans are failing. Every summer, as temperatures climb past 45 degrees, we read the same headlines about deaths in our cities, and every summer officials point to plans that look good on paper. The truth is that these plans are not reaching the people who need them most.'

Then I go through the findings roughly in the order above.

Two colleagues gave me opposite advice. One says lead with the 38% because editors like good news and it keeps officials onside. The other says lead with informal workers because that's the human story. Which finding should I lead with, and what's the argument that actually ties these together?

title: Library fines essay, editor confused me
prompt:
Hello, I'm a branch librarian in Dublin and I've written an essay for a library sector newsletter, and maybe an Irish Times opinion pitch if it's good enough. Topic: the fines-free policy our libraries brought in back in 2019 and why other library systems should follow. My editor's only note was 'you're arguing the wrong thing.' She's away for two weeks so I can't ask what she meant. Can you see it? I'm also unsure how to end it.

DRAFT:

Library fines are, at bottom, a tax on the poor. They are a relic of a Victorian idea that working people must be disciplined into respecting property, and every euro collected is a small act of class warfare against the very people public libraries were built to serve. This is why abolishing them matters.

When Dublin's public libraries went fines-free in 2019, critics predicted chaos: books would vanish, shelves would empty, standards would collapse.

At my own branch, the share of items returned within six weeks went from 91% before the change to 94% after. We had been collecting about €4,200 a year in fines, while staff spent an estimated nine hours a week processing fines, chasing them and handling disputes at the desk. In the first year, 340 lapsed borrowers rejoined, most of them either under 18 or over 65. One man in his seventies told me he had stayed away for twelve years over a €6 fine on a children's book his late wife had borrowed for their grandson.

Opponents will say that without fines there is no accountability. But accountability to whom? The library is a commons, not a shop. Those who defend fines are, whether they know it or not, defending a system designed to keep the poor in their place.

Other countries still cling to fines out of habit and a kind of moral squeamishness. It is time they caught up.

(end)

About 380 words now, the newsletter allows up to 900, so there's room if something needs adding.
